rules.window_note: The optical parts of Nikon binoculars, rangefinding binoculars and fieldscopes are covered for the life of the product. The other parts get 7 years and any electronics get 1 year; Nikon rangefinders get 5 years. It has to be bought new from a Nikon Authorized Dealer, and refurbished ones get 90 days.
rules.what_you_get: A claim for a defect in materials or workmanship under Nikon's lifetime limited warranty for binoculars.
rules.how_to_claim: Keep your dated receipt and contact Nikon support to arrange service.
rules.script_hint: The optics on my Nikon binoculars have a defect, and Nikon's lifetime limited warranty covers the optical parts for the life of the product.

rules.what_you_get: A free repair, parts and labour included. Nikon can choose to replace it instead.
rules.how_to_claim: Take it back to the shop you bought it from, or to a Nikon authorised service centre, with the warranty card and receipt.
rules.script_hint: My Nikon [item] is less than a year old and has a manufacturing defect, so it's covered by Nikon's service warranty; here are my receipt and warranty card.
rules.source_quote: Your Nikon equipment is guaranteed against any manufacturing defects for one full year from the date of original purchase.

rules.title: New NIKKOR Z lenses get 5 years in the UK if you register them
rules.window_note: Register a new NIKKOR Z mount lens within 90 days of buying it and it is covered for five years. You need a Nikon Store account, the lens serial number and your proof of purchase. Accidental damage, loss and theft aren't covered.
rules.what_you_get: Free repairs by Nikon approved technicians if the lens develops a fault.
rules.how_to_claim: Sign in to your Nikon Store account, register the lens with its serial number and receipt, and keep the warranty certificate Nikon sends you. Show it when you contact Nikon about a fault.
rules.script_hint: I registered my NIKKOR Z lens within 90 days, so it's covered by Nikon's five-year extended warranty, and it now has a fault.
rules.source_quote: register your lens within 90 days of purchase and it will be covered against faults (terms and conditions apply) that may occur within the first five years, with free repairs.

rules.how_to_claim: Ship the camera with tracking to FUJIFILM North America, Attn: Camera Repair Dept., 1100 King Georges Post Road, Edison, NJ 08837. Put in a copy of your dated receipt, a note on the problem with your phone, address and email, and the repair form from camerarepair.fujifilmusa.com. Don't send batteries or accessories.
rules.script_hint: My Fujifilm camera is under a year old and has a fault, so it's covered by Fujifilm's one-year limited warranty; a copy of my dated receipt is enclosed.
rules.source_quote: A copy of a dated proof of purchase (Limited one year warranty on all Fujifilm digital cameras from date of purchase)

Drops, water, sand, and repairs by anyone else aren't covered.
rules.what_you_get: A free repair of a manufacturing defect. If Fujifilm finds nothing wrong, it may charge a $25 diagnostic fee.
rules.how_to_claim: Call Fujifilm technical support first. Then take or send it, with your receipt, back to the store or website you bought it from, or mail it to FUJIFILM Canada Inc., 600 Suffolk Court, Mississauga, ON L5R 4G4, Attention: Camera Repair. You pay to send it; the trip back is paid if it has a real defect.
rules.script_hint: My Fujifilm camera has a manufacturing defect and is under a year old, so it's covered by Fujifilm Canada's one-year warranty; here's my receipt.

rules.title: GoPro cameras get 1 year
rules.window_note: One year from the day it was delivered to you, against manufacturing defects. Damage from use, accidents or normal wear isn't covered, and neither is water leaking into a housing you sealed yourself. GoPro has a separate policy for the EU.
rules.what_you_get: GoPro repairs or replaces the faulty part or camera with a comparable one, free of charge. GoPro may choose to cover the shipping.
rules.how_to_claim: Contact GoPro Customer Support at gopro.com/help before sending anything. If they agree it's a warranty problem they give you an RMA number; write it on the box and ship it to the address they give you. Don't drop it off in person.
rules.script_hint: My GoPro has a manufacturing defect and was delivered less than a year ago, so it's covered by GoPro's one-year warranty; please issue an RMA.
rules.source_quote: GoPro products are guaranteed against manufacturing defects one (1) year from the original date of delivery. GoPro's sole obligation in the event of such defects during this period is to repair or replace the defective part or product

rules.what_you_get: GoPro repairs or replaces a defective mount or accessory.
rules.how_to_claim: Get a return authorization at gopro.com/help before shipping. Send it prepaid and insured, with a note explaining the problem and your receipt.
rules.script_hint: This GoPro mount has a defect, and non-electrical GoPro mounts carry a lifetime warranty, so I'd like it repaired or replaced.
rules.source_quote: Non-electrical GoPro mounts and accessories* are covered by a Lifetime Warranty against defects in materials and workmanship for the product's lifetime for the benefit of the first purchaser or gift recipient.

notes:
COVERAGE: 25 manufacturer-warranty rules, all read from primary sources this session (the brand's own warranty page, warranty PDF, or official help-centre article). No settlements, card benefits or statutory rules here — this batch is manufacturer warranties only.

WHAT I VERIFIED DIRECTLY (confidence "certain"): Apple, Google, Bose, Dyson, DeWalt (both rules), Milwaukee, Lodge, Le Creuset, Vitamix, YETI, Stanley 1913, Osprey, Patagonia, Darn Tough, Nike, Timex, Whirlpool, L.L.Bean. For each of these I read the actual warranty text stating the term and the remedy.

WEAKER SPOTS (confidence "likely" — read these before publishing):
- LG TV: the 1-year parts-and-labour term comes from LG's own printed "LG LCD / LED / OLED Television Limited Warranty - USA" document, which I found mirrored on a retailer's site rather than on lg.com. LG's own site only offers a model-number lookup tool (the source_url I used), so I could not re-verify the term on an lg.com page. The term is very likely right but the source link doesn't state it on its face.
- GE Appliances: geappliances.com has no single current "warranty" landing page I could find; I verified the one-year parts-and-labour pattern from a GE-hosted warranty PDF, which is an older document. The phone number (1-800-432-2737) is from geappliances.com's own contact page. Treat "one year" as the general pattern, not a guarantee for every model.
- Samsung: samsung.com/us/support/warranty states the standard limited warranty is 1 year but does not break it out by product type on the US page. Samsung's Canadian site lists 12 months for phones, tablets, wearables, TVs, laptops and home appliances, which is consistent.
- Dell: Dell's warranty length genuinely varies (90 days to 5+ years) and is printed on the invoice. I set 12 months as the common consumer default and said so plainly in window_note. Do not present "1 year" as certain for Dell.
- KitchenAid: the one-year hassle-free stand-mixer replacement is stated on kitchenaid.com, but I could not open the linked warranty PDF (timed out) to confirm the exact wording. I left contact as the support page rather than invent a phone number.
- JanSport: fetched from jansport.com but via a summarising fetch rather than raw page text, so some phrasing may be paraphrased. Core terms (limited lifetime, defects only, not wear and tear) are consistent with their published policy.

DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT:
- Craftsman lifetime hand-tool warranty. Widely believed and probably still true, but craftsman.com's warranty page renders its terms in collapsed accordions that I could not extract, and the only concrete statements I found were retailer pages and forum posts. Rather than guess a term for a brand where the warranty has genuinely changed hands (Sears to Stanley Black & Decker) and where customers report inconsistent honouring, I dropped it. Worth a second pass with a browser that can expand the accordions.
- iRobot / Roomba one-year warranty. iRobot's own pages state it, but I saw multiple 2026 references to an iRobot bankruptcy. A warranty from a company in bankruptcy proceedings may not actually pay out, and telling someone to rely on it could waste their time. Needs a fresh check of iRobot's status before including.
- Shark, Anker, Sony, HP, Lenovo, console makers, mattress and bike brands — not researched in this batch, not omitted for any negative reason.

BLANK CONTACTS ARE INTENTIONAL: Whirlpool and L.L.Bean have empty contact fields because I did not verify a phone number for them in a primary source. Per the honesty rule I left them blank rather than reproduce a number from memory. Both how_to_claim fields still tell the person exactly what to do.

TWO GOTCHAS WORTH SURFACING IN THE UI:
1. Nike's clock runs from the MANUFACTURE date on the tag, not the purchase date. People lose this warranty without realising.
2. Dyson's clock starts 90 days after manufacture if you have no receipt, and Dyson will reject claims on machines bought from unauthorised sellers (including most Amazon third-party sellers).

REGIONS: almost everything here is scoped to US because I read the US-specific warranty documents. Several of these brands offer similar or better terms in the EU/UK, where statutory rights add a separate two-year layer — that belongs in a statutory-rules batch, not this one.

COVERAGE AND SOURCING

Every rule above was read from a primary or issuer-published benefit document, not from a blog summary. Sources used: Visa's own terms PDFs on usa.visa.com (purchase security and extended warranty, effective 4/15/21); the American Express US Extended Warranty, Purchase Protection and Return Protection benefit guides on americanexpress.com (rev. 4/19/2024, 10/2020 editions); Amex Bank of Canada's Certificate of Insurance (amended and restated effective 1 July 2025); Mastercard Guide to Benefits booklets published by a credit union (core credit) and by Capital One (World Elite); Chase's own education pages; Canadian Tire's Triangle World Elite certificate booklet; Scotiabank's Visa Infinite purchase security certificate.

THE BIG HONEST CAVEAT: WHETHER A GIVEN CARD HAS THE BENEFIT AT ALL

Visa and Mastercard set the standard terms, but each bank decides whether to include them. So a rule marked "likely" means the terms are verified but you cannot promise that any particular Visa or Mastercard carries the benefit. The product should tell users to look up their own card's Guide to Benefits rather than assert coverage. Amex is the exception: Amex is both issuer and network, so its terms are marked "certain", though Amex still says only "eligible cards" qualify (return protection in particular sits on fewer cards, which is why it is marked "likely").

CARDS THAT DROPPED THESE BENEFITS (verified, useful as negative answers)
- Discover: ended extended warranty, purchase protection and return guarantee on 28 February 2018. Discover is the one major US network with none of these. Answer for Discover users should be "your card does not cover this, but the manufacturer or a state law might".
- Citi: cut extended warranty, damage and theft purchase protection, 90-day return protection and Price Rewind on 22 September 2019, then added a 24-month extended warranty back to some cards (Double Cash, Custom Cash) from 17 November 2024. Citi also removed extended warranty from the Costco card around early 2023. Citi is the messiest issuer to reason about.
- Capital One QuickSilver Mastercard: lost extended warranty and price protection from 1 September 2021 (reporting suggested the Visa version may have been unaffected — unverified).
- Chase dropped price protection and return protection across all cards in 2018 but kept purchase protection and extended warranty.
- Amex halved its extended warranty from 2 extra years to 1 extra year for purchases made from 1 October 2020.
- Price protection is effectively dead everywhere: Visa and Mastercard ended their network programs in 2018. Do not build price-drop refunds into the product.

DETAILS I COULD NOT PIN DOWN
- The Visa benefit administrator phone number differs by issuer. Visa's own current PDFs use 1-888-221-3289 and cardbenefitservices.com; some issuer guides (e.g. UBS, Bank of America) still print 1-800-397-9010. The safest instruction is "call the number on the back of your card". I used Visa's own number and said so.
- Mastercard purchase assurance caps vary a lot by card ($1,000 per loss on the Capital One World Elite guide I read; other issuers differ). I stated the number I verified and flagged that it varies.
- I did not verify a live Citi Guide to Protection Benefits PDF: the cardbenefits.citi.com link I tried returned "item not found", so the Citi numbers come from a mirrored copy of Citi's May 2024 guide. Citi's claim reporting wording in that document is "as soon as possible after the Incident" with documents due within 180 days — I did not find a hard day count for first notice, so I did not invent one. Citi is marked "likely" and its source_url points at Citi's live benefits site rather than the mirror.
- I could not read the Visa Signature PDF directly (encoding failure), so the Signature terms were confirmed through an issuer-hosted copy of the same Visa language and are described together with Infinite, whose Visa-hosted PDF I did read in full. The two are identical on every number I checked.
- Amex US purchase protection and extended warranty both require Notice of Claim "within thirty (30) days of the loss or as soon as reasonably possible". The 30-day figure is explicit in the extended warranty guide and on Amex's own credit-intel page; in the purchase protection PDF that clause was garbled by text extraction, so I carried the same 30 days across but flag it here.
- Canadian terms vary by issuer more than US ones. Purchase security notice deadlines I found range from 30 days (RBC's Visa Infinite wording, seen only in search results) to 45 days (Scotiabank, read in full) to 90 days (Triangle Mastercard, read in full). Amex Canada's 48-hour reporting rule is real and read directly from the July 2025 certificate — it is the single most missable deadline in this whole set and is worth surfacing loudly.

WHAT I DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT
- Price protection and Citi Price Rewind: discontinued.
- Wells Fargo: widely reported to have no extended warranty on any card, but I did not find a Wells Fargo primary document saying so, so I made no rule and no claim.
- Cell phone protection: a real and valuable card benefit, but it is a separate product from the three you asked about and usually requires paying the phone bill with the card.
- Category lists are my judgement about what these benefits normally cover, not quoted from the documents. Every one of these benefits excludes motor vehicles, software, consumables, live plants and animals, used or refurbished goods, and anything bought for business resale. E-bikes and motorised scooters are explicitly excluded in the Amex Canada certificate, so "bike" is omitted there.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANGLE
Extended warranty is the strongest fit for the landfill story: it pays for a repair on an item the maker has stopped standing behind, and the documents literally require a repair estimate from an authorised shop before they will replace anything. Purchase protection is more often a payout than a repair.

COVERAGE: 13 rules, every one checked against the actual settlement administrator site, manufacturer support page, or government source — not against aggregator blogs. Aggregators were only used to find candidates.

WHAT I DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED (all were candidates that failed verification):
- Mitsubishi ACU settlement — acusettlement.com/mitsubishi states the claim deadline PASSED on 23 May 2026. Closed.
- Shimano defective crankset settlement — deadline was 4 Aug 2026. Already closed.
- Honda/Acura DENSO fuel pump settlement (15yr/150k warranty extension) — this is only a PROPOSED settlement as of April 2026. I found no final approval and no official claim site, so I left it out rather than publish a deadline I could not confirm.
- Nintendo Joy-Con drift free repair — very widely reported and probably real, but Nintendo's own support answer page (a_id/41693) now returns "This answer is no longer available." I could not verify it from any Nintendo-owned page, so I dropped it rather than record an unverifiable policy.

CONFLICT I RESOLVED: aggregators disagreed on the Hyundai/Kia airbag deadline (29 March 2027 vs 8 April 2027). The administrator's own site states 8 April 2027 in four separate places. I used 8 April 2027.

TIME-SENSITIVE: the BMW shark-fin claim deadline is 27 August 2026 — one day after this research was done. The cash-back part will be dead almost immediately, but the extended warranty survives it and needs no claim form, so the rule is still worth keeping. Reword the UI copy once that date passes.

DELIBERATE DESIGN CHOICE: the two strongest rules here (Hyundai and Kia engine) have expired CASH deadlines but LIVE warranty extensions requiring no paperwork. Those are worth more to a real user than most open settlements, and Owed should surface that distinction — "the money window closed, the free-repair window did not."

KNOWN WEAK SPOTS:
- BMW: the specific reimbursement caps (100% uncapped at a BMW dealer, 100% up to $2,000 at an independent shop) and the 10-year/120,000-mile figure come from secondary reporting. The administrator homepage confirms reimbursement and a warranty extension exist but does not print those numbers. I wrote what_you_get to only claim what the primary source supports. Read the long-form notice PDF before showing dollar figures to users.
- California secret warranty rule is marked "likely" not "certain": the statute plainly exists and multiple legal databases agree, but I verified the 2-year and 21-business-day details through california.public.law rather than the official Legislative Counsel site.
- contact is intentionally EMPTY on all Apple rules and on the NHTSA rule. Apple routes these through a web flow and printed no phone number on the pages I read; I did not want to paste a support number I had not seen on the verified page. Same for NHTSA's hotline.
- The category vocabulary has no "vehicle" value, so six vehicle rules are tagged "other". If Owed is going to lean on cars — and it should, since car rules carry the biggest money — that vocabulary needs a "vehicle" category.

SCOPE: everything here is US except the Apple programmes, which Apple describes as worldwide (I marked the three-prong adapter UK, since that is the plug style it covers). Nothing here is verified for Canada, the UK or the EU specifically, and the two statutory rules (NHTSA, CPSC) are US-only by definition.

FRESHNESS: settlement deadlines move and service programmes get retired. Every rule here should be re-checked against its source_url on a schedule — the Apple pages carry an "Information as of" date, and the settlement sites publish key-dates pages that are cheap to re-scrape.

15 rules, all statutory (consumer law that beats the printed warranty). Verification method and honest caveats:

WHAT I VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCES (fetched and read the actual text):
- 15 U.S.C. 2302(c), 2308, 2310(d) and 16 CFR 700.10 via Cornell LII — the anti-tying rule, the disclaimer ban, and the attorney-fee provision are quoted from statute.
- UK Consumer Rights Act 2015 Part 1 Ch. 2 via legislation.gov.uk — 30-day right to reject (s.22), satisfactory quality incl. durability (s.9), six-month presumption (s.19(14)).
- California Civil Code 1791.1(c), 1793.2(d) and 1793.03 via leginfo.legislature.ca.gov — the 60-day/1-year implied warranty, the replace-or-refund duty, and the 3-year/7-year parts rule.
- BC Sale of Goods Act ss.18(c) and 20(2) via bclaws.gov.bc.ca — the durability condition and the void-waiver rule.
- Colorado HB24-1121 via leg.colorado.gov — the 1 Jan 2026 date and the parts-pairing ban wording.
- Minnesota Stat. 325E.72 via revisor.mn.gov — the "fair and reasonable terms" duty and the ban on requiring pairing/registration.
- EU legal guarantee via europa.eu Your Europe (official EU citizen portal) — 2 years minimum, 1-year reversed burden of proof, claim lies against the seller.
- Quebec legal warranty via Éducaloi — arts. 37/38, claimable against merchant OR manufacturer, free, survives the printed warranty.
- OPC phone (1 888 672-2556) and Citizens Advice consumer helpline (0808 223 1133) both verified on their own sites. FTC reporting URL verified.

WHERE I HAD TO RELY ON SECONDARY SOURCES:
- EUR-Lex and ftc.gov both blocked full-text fetching (403 / empty extraction). For the EU Right to Repair Directive 2024/1799 I cross-checked three independent sources (Right to Repair Europe, Freshfields on the German implementing bill, EUR-Lex's own summary page) and they agree on: producer duty to repair Annex II goods at a reasonable price outside the guarantee, the one-off 12-month extension when you choose repair over replacement, and the 31 July 2026 transposition deadline. For the FTC material I relied on FTC-domain search results describing their own pages plus the underlying statute, which I did read.
- Quebec's warranty of good working order durations come from Osler's summary of the published regulation, not the regulation text itself. Marked certain because the durations were consistent across Osler, Stikeman and McCarthy, but the source_url is a law firm page rather than a statute.
- EU ecodesign 2023/1670 specifics (7 years, 5-10 working days, 800 cycles, 5 years of OS updates, 15 parts to repairers) come from consistent secondary reporting; the EUR-Lex text itself would not extract. source_url points at the European Commission's own product page.

DELIBERATE HONESTY CHOICES:
- I left `contact` empty on five rules rather than guess at an Attorney General complaint URL or a company line I had not confirmed.
- `us-implied-warranty-merchantability` is marked "likely" only because the four-year window is UCC 2-725 as adopted by most states — a handful differ, and I did not audit all 50.
- `ca-durability-implied-warranty` is marked "likely" because I verified BC's wording directly but generalised "most provinces have a similar rule" without checking each one; the roughly-two-year court deadline is a general statement, not a per-province check.
- `eu-right-to-repair-directive` is marked "likely" because Right to Repair Europe explicitly stated that as of the 31 July 2026 deadline several member states had not finished transposing, so a given user's country may not have it live yet.
- Quebec's warranty of good working order does not start until 5 October 2026 (about six weeks after today). I included it because it is fully enacted with published durations, but the window_note says plainly when it starts. I did not verify whether it reaches goods bought before that date, so I avoided claiming either way.

GAPS I DID NOT FILL:
- No `deadline` values are set — none of these are settlements, so none have claim deadlines.
- Washington state's electronics repair law appeared in search results but I could not confirm its effective date, so I left it out entirely rather than name it.
- Saskatchewan and New Brunswick let consumers claim directly against manufacturers, which is unusually strong, but it is single-province coverage and I did not verify it to primary-source level, so it is not included.
- I did not name which specific five spare parts must go to end-users under the EU phone rules, because I could only confirm the count, not the list.
